memoryText: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; it is to him you shall listen.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Deuteronomy 18:15 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Deuteronomy 18:15 is a promise and a command in a single sentence. It was spoken by Moses near the end of his life, and it is quoted in the New Testament as a promise fulfilled in Jesus.

“The LORD your God will raise up for you.” The prophet is a gift from God. He is not self-appointed. God takes the initiative to speak to his people, and he does it by raising up someone for them. The whole idea of revelation begins with God.

“A prophet like me.” Moses was the greatest prophet of the Old Testament. God spoke with him face to face. He mediated the covenant, performed signs, led the people out of Egypt, and gave the law. To be “like Moses” is a high standard. Deuteronomy 34:10 says that no prophet had yet arisen like him. The promise looks beyond the line of ordinary prophets to someone who would be like Moses, and greater.

“From among you, from your brothers.” The prophet will be one of them. He is a true human being, a member of the covenant family. This points to the incarnation, in which God’s Son became a man.

“It is to him you shall listen.” The command is simple: listen. The Father said the same thing at the transfiguration, when Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Mark 9:7). The prophet like Moses has come, and he is the Son.

To be a Christian is to be a listener of Jesus. Spend today in quiet listening. Read the Gospels slowly, and ask him to speak.
weekInReview: This week you read more of Moses’ sermons in Deuteronomy. You saw that the Lord’s election of Israel was not based on their righteousness, and you read of the golden calf and Moses’ intercession again. You prayed through the second half of Psalm 78, which ends with the choice of David as shepherd. You read laws about worship, false prophets, the tithe, the release of debts, and the care of the poor, and you studied the three offices of Christ as prophet, priest, and king. You read the law of the king and the promise of a prophet like Moses, and a long series of laws about justice, warfare, and daily life. You read the firstfruits creed, the covenant ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim, and the first blessings of obedience. The week taught that God’s law shapes every part of life, and that all of Israel’s offices find their fulfillment in Christ.
reflectionQuestions: Moses promised a prophet like himself, and Jesus is that prophet. What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and listening to him?
The three offices of prophet, priest, and king show different sides of Christ’s work. Which of the three do you most need to lean on at this stage of your life, and why?
The firstfruits creed ends with rejoicing in “all the good that the LORD your God has given.” What good things has God given you that you have not stopped to thank him for?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus as your prophet, priest, and king.
Ask him to speak today and to help you listen.
